title: Let There Be
sum: Before anything else, God. Out of a dark, shapeless, watery deep, God speaks, and light, sky, sea, land, plants, lights, birds, fish and land animals come to be, each "by its kind," each called "good." On the sixth day God makes humankind, male and female, "in our image, as our likeness," blesses them, and gives them the earth to rule and fill. Then he looks at everything he has made and calls it "very good."

The chapter is built like a hymn, with repeated lines and a careful pattern of days. How literally to read those days has been argued since ancient times, and the argument grew sharper with modern geology and biology. Jews and Christians who disagree about the days still agree on what the chapter says about God: one Creator, sovereign, good, who makes by his word, and who gives human beings a dignity no other ancient text gave them.
readings: Read as history

Most Jews and Christians through history, and young-earth creationists today, read the chapter as a straightforward account of what happened in six ordinary days, a few thousand years ago. Old-earth readers also read it as history, but allow that the days or the time between them may be long. Either way, the order of events and the act of creation are real.
Read as a picture of the world as God's temple

Many scholars read the chapter as the ancient Near East would have heard it: a cosmos ordered and assigned its functions, ending with God at rest on the seventh day like a king enthroned in a finished temple. The week is real, but its subject is purpose, not physics.
Read as Israel's answer to Babylon

Critical scholars read the chapter as written or shaped by Israel's priests, perhaps during the exile, to answer the Babylonian creation epic: no war among gods, no worship of sun and moon, and humans as royal images rather than slaves of the gods. The chapter is theology in the form of a cosmology.

views.L: Six ordinary days, as the evening-and-morning refrain and Exodus 20:11 indicate, about six thousand years ago by the genealogies. Light on day one came from God before the sun (compare Revelation 22:5). Animals and humans were vegetarian (1:29–30), and death came only with sin. Science should be read in light of Scripture, not the reverse.
views.O: The events are real and in order, but the days are long ages (Hugh Ross), or God's own work-days told by analogy (C. John Collins), or ordinary days separated by long periods. Day four may describe the sun becoming visible from the earth's surface, not its creation. The heavens and earth of 1:1 may be very old.
views.F: The week is a literary frame. Days one to three create realms (light and dark, sea and sky, land), and days four to six fill them with rulers (lights, birds and fish, animals and humans). Augustine already read the days as non-chronological; Arie Noordtzij, Meredith Kline and Henri Blocher developed the framework view; John Walton reads it as the dedication of the cosmos as God's temple. The chapter teaches who made the world and why, not when or how.
views.C: Most critical scholars assign 1:1–2:3 to the Priestly source, usually dated to the 500s BC (some, such as Kaufmann and Milgrom, date it before the exile), and read it against Mesopotamian cosmology: a flat earth, a solid dome holding back waters above, and seas below. The writer meant ordinary days, but the purpose is theological: one God, a good creation, the Sabbath built into the world, and humans as God's images.
views.J: Many rabbis and medieval commentators read the days as ordinary days, but the tradition never fixed one view. Genesis Rabbah says God "was building worlds and destroying them" before this one (3:7; 9:2); Maimonides warned that not everything in the account is meant in its plain sense (Guide 2.29–30); Nachmanides read the six days also as six thousand years of history (on 2:3); and modern Orthodox thinkers (Rav Kook; Aryeh Kaplan, citing Isaac of Acre; Gerald Schroeder) accept an ancient universe. Rashi asks why the Torah begins with creation at all, and answers that the whole earth belongs to God, who gives it to whom he pleases. The Mishnah restricts public teaching of the "work of creation" (Hagigah 2:1).

deep.h: The days of creation: six readings in their strongest form
deep.b:
1. Ordinary days. The plainest reading of yom with a number and "evening and morning" is a normal day. Exodus 20:11 builds the work week on it: "in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth." Jesus speaks of humans made "from the beginning of creation" (Mark 10:6). Most church fathers, the Reformers and Archbishop Ussher read the days this way, and young-earth creationists (Henry Morris, Ken Ham, Jonathan Sarfati) hold that science must be reinterpreted to fit.

2. Day-age. Yom can mean a period (2:4; Isaiah 2:12). The sixth day holds a great deal: naming the animals, a deep sleep, the woman's creation (2:7–23). The seventh day has no end, and Hebrews 4 treats it as still open. The order of creation broadly matches the order in modern science (Hugh Ross).

3. Analogical days. The days are God's work-days, like a craftsman's week but not measured by human clocks; their pattern is the model for Israel's week (C. John Collins).

4. Framework. Light comes before the sun, and days four to six mirror days one to three; the arrangement is topical. Genesis 2:5 assumes ordinary providence (no rain, so no plants), which Kline argued rules out a creation in 144 hours.

5. Cosmic temple. In the ancient world temples were dedicated over seven days and a god "rested" in his finished temple. Genesis 1 is about functions given to the cosmos, not the making of matter (John Walton).

6. Gap. An undated first creation in 1:1, ruined and remade (Chalmers; the Scofield Bible). Most scholars now reject it on grammatical grounds.

Many readers, from medieval commentators to modern ones, have noticed that the days fall into two matching sets of three.

Day 1: light and darkness / Day 4: sun, moon and stars.
Day 2: sky and waters below / Day 5: birds and sea creatures.
Day 3: dry land and plants / Day 6: land animals and humans, with plants for food.

The first three days answer "shapeless" (tohu) by forming spaces; the last three answer "empty" (bohu) by filling them. The seventh day stands alone. Framework readers say the pattern shows the order is topical; others reply that a pattern can also be chronological.

deep.title: Enuma Elish: the Babylonian creation epic
deep.b: In the Enuma Elish, known from copies of the first millennium BC, the fresh waters (Apsu) and salt sea (Tiamat) mingle and give birth to the gods. War breaks out; the young god Marduk kills Tiamat, splits her body like a fish, and sets half of it up as the sky with guards so her waters cannot escape. He makes the stars and the calendar, then creates humans from the blood of a rebel god so that they can do the gods' work, and the gods build Babylon and its temple for him. Shared features with Genesis 1: a dark, watery beginning; a dividing of waters above and below; the heavenly bodies set for time; humans made last; and a god at rest in a temple. The differences go to the root: one God, not many; no birth of gods and no battle; humans as God's image and rulers, not slaves. Most scholars see Genesis 1 as speaking into this world of ideas, whether or not its writer knew this exact text.

James Ussher, the Irish archbishop, dated creation to the evening before 23 October 4004 BC (Julian calendar) in his Annals of 1650, using the Hebrew numbers of Genesis 5 and 11 and later biblical and historical chronology. Other scholars of his day reached similar dates. Christians who used the Greek Septuagint, such as Eusebius, had reached dates over 5,000 BC, and the Jewish calendar, counting from creation, places it in 3761 BC.

deep.title: "Good" missing on day two, "very good" on day six
deep.body: My own idea, building on the rabbis' observation (Genesis Rabbah 4:6): the refrain "it was good" seems to come when a work is complete. Day two only divides the waters; the work with the waters is not finished until the seas are gathered on day three, which gets "good" twice (1:10, 12). Likewise humans are not called "good" by themselves on day six; only "everything" together is "very good" (1:31). Read this way, the chapter's idea of goodness is about completed wholes, not separate parts, which fits the later "not good" of the man alone (2:18).

echoes: John 1:1–5; Psalm 8:3–8; Psalm 33:6–9; Psalm 104:1–35; Psalm 136:5–9; Proverbs 8:22–31; Job 38:4–11; Isaiah 40:26; Isaiah 45:18; Jeremiah 4:23–26; Exodus 20:11; Mark 10:6; 2 Corinthians 4:6; Colossians 1:15–17; Hebrews 11:3; Revelation 21:1–5

settings.what: God's blessing on the creatures of sea and sky
settings.to: The sea creatures and the birds made on the fifth day
settings.why: The first blessing in the Bible: be fruitful, grow many, fill the waters and the earth. God's blessing here is the power of life to go on making life.
settings.readers: For Israel the word "bless" begins here and runs through the whole book. The same blessing is given to humankind (1:28), to Noah (9:1) and to Abraham's family (17:6; 35:11). Israel learned that its own growth in Egypt (Exodus 1:7) was the Creator's first blessing at work.

settings.what: God's blessing and charge to humankind
settings.to: The first man and woman, the humankind he has just made in his image
settings.when: On the sixth day, after the land animals
settings.why: To give human beings their place and work in the world. They are to be fruitful, fill the earth and rule it as God's images, and to take the plants for food. Male and female alike bear his image.
settings.readers: For Israel, in a world where kings were called the image of a god, this gave every human being a king's dignity. Hearing it after slavery in Egypt or exile in Babylon, Israel learned that no Pharaoh or emperor owned them. They and their masters alike bore God's image.
views: Many scholars (Middleton, Walton) read the image as a calling: humans stand for God in the world, as a king's statue stood for him in a province.
Much Jewish and Christian tradition read the image as reason, freedom or the ability to know God.

traditions.q: What is the image of God in human beings, and did the fall destroy it?
views: The image is the spiritual soul, with reason and free will, which makes every person able to know and love God (Catechism 357, 1703–1705). Sin wounded human nature but did not destroy the image, and grace heals and raises it.

Following Irenaeus, the Orthodox separate the image from the likeness (1:26). Every person keeps the image as a gift that cannot be lost; the likeness is the goal, a lifelong growth into God's life by grace, which the Orthodox call theosis.

Luther taught that the image was Adam's original righteousness: knowing God truly, trusting him and loving him. In that sense the image was lost in the fall and is restored only in Christ, though human beings remain human and not a substance of sin (Formula of Concord, article 1).

Calvin held that the image was not wholly wiped out but so corrupted that what is left is badly deformed (Institutes 1.15.4). The Westminster Confession describes the image as knowledge, righteousness and true holiness, which Christ renews in believers (Colossians 3:10; Ephesians 4:24).

title: Dust, Breath and a Garden
sum: The week of creation ends with a day that God blesses and makes holy, because on it he stopped from all his work. Then the story begins again, closer to the ground. The LORD God shapes a man from the soil, breathes life into him, and plants a garden in Eden with every good tree, the tree of life and the tree of knowing good and evil. He sets the man there to work it and guard it, with one command: do not eat from the tree of knowing good and evil.

For the first time something is "not good": the man is alone. God parades the animals before him to name, but none is his match. So God builds a woman from the man's side and brings her to him, and the man bursts into the Bible's first poem. The narrator adds that this is why a man leaves his parents and sticks close to his wife. The chapter ends with the two of them naked and unashamed.
readings: Read as history

The traditional reading takes the garden, the man, the woman and the trees as real, in a real place watered by real rivers. Chapter 2 is a close-up of the sixth day, giving the details of how God made the first couple.
Read as a sanctuary story

Many scholars read the garden as the first temple: God walks there, the man serves and guards it like a priest, and gold, onyx and cherubim belong to sanctuary imagery. Humans were made to live in God's presence.
Read as a second source

Critical scholars read 2:4b–25 as the Yahwist's creation story, older than chapter 1, with a different style and order. Its interest is the human condition: work, desire, companionship and the limits set by God.

views.L: The six days are summarized in 2:1–3, and 2:4–25 fills in day six in detail. Adam was the first human, made directly from dust, and Eve was made from his rib. Eden was a real place, though the flood may have changed its geography.
views.O: Most old-earth readers also hold to a historical Adam and Eve as the first couple or as the heads of humanity, specially created. Some allow that God formed the man from earlier life. The "day" of 2:4 shows that yom can mean a longer time.
views.F: The garden is a sanctuary and the man its priest (2:15). The story uses images, a potter, a garden, a rib, to teach who humans are: made of earth, alive by God's breath, made for work, for God and for each other. John Walton reads Adam and Eve as real people presented as archetypes of all humanity.
views.C: Critical scholars assign 2:4b–3:24 to the Yahwist (J), traditionally dated to the 900s BC, though many now date it later. It is a story of origins, like Atrahasis, explaining work, marriage, shame and death. The geography combines real rivers with legendary ones.
views.J: The rabbis saw God as a matchmaker who adorned Eve and brought her to Adam (Genesis Rabbah 18:1). They read "helper who is his match" as "if he is worthy, she helps him; if not, she opposes him" (Rashi, from Yevamot 63a). The Sabbath of 2:1–3 is recited every Friday evening in the Kiddush blessing over wine.

deep.h: How the two creation accounts fit
deep.b: Chapter 1 moves from chaos to order, uses "God" only, and ends with humankind and rest. Chapter 2 starts with a dry land without plants or farmers, uses "the LORD God," and moves from the man to the garden, the animals and the woman. Source critics see two independent accounts with different orders. Traditional readers point out that 2:5 speaks of plants "of the field" (crops that need farming and rain), not all plants; that the animals of 2:19 may have been formed earlier ("had shaped"); and that ancient writers often gave a summary followed by a detailed retelling (Kitchen; Collins). Literary readers note that the final editor deliberately set the two side by side, one cosmic and one personal, as two views of the same truth.

deep.title: Humans from clay
deep.b: Many ancient peoples said humans were made from clay. In Atrahasis the birth goddess mixes clay with the flesh and blood of a slain god, and the gods spit on it; humans are made to carry the gods' workload. In Egyptian art the god Khnum shapes people on a potter's wheel. Genesis shares the picture of the divine potter but gives it a new sense: the man is made to tend God's garden and receives God's own breath, not a dead god's blood.

Genesis 2:24 became the foundation text for marriage in both Judaism and Christianity. Jesus joined it with 1:27 to answer a question about divorce (Matthew 19:3–9), and Paul used it to describe Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32). In Jewish weddings, the seven blessings (sheva berakhot) recall God's joy over the first couple in Eden.

deep.title: The man names the animals but not himself
deep.body: My own observation, which overlaps with comments by Robert Alter and others on naming: in chapter 2 the man names every animal, but the text never has him name himself, and when he names the woman he names himself in the same breath (ishshah from ish, 2:23). His own identity comes only in relation to her. Naming the animals shows his rule over them; failing to find a match among them shows that rule is not enough for a human. The first human self-description is relational.

echoes: Exodus 20:8–11; Exodus 31:17; Psalm 103:14; Job 33:4; Ecclesiastes 12:7; Ezekiel 28:13–14; Ezekiel 47:1–12; Matthew 19:4–6; Mark 10:6–9; 1 Corinthians 11:8–12; 1 Corinthians 15:45–47; Ephesians 5:31–32; Hebrews 4:3–10; Revelation 22:1–2

settings.to: The man, alone in the garden of Eden, before the woman is made
settings.when: After God settles him in the garden to work it and guard it
settings.why: To give the man freedom with one limit. Every tree is his except the tree of knowing good and evil, and eating from it means death. A single command makes trust and obedience possible. The woman later repeats it with an addition (3:3).
settings.readers: For Israel, given a good land and many commands at Sinai, Adam's choice was its own. It could have life in the land by listening to God, or exile from it.
views: Many readers see Eden and Israel's story as matched: a land given, a command, disobedience, and being sent out to the east.

settings.what: The man's poem over the woman
settings.to: The woman God has just built from his side and brought to him
settings.why: The Bible's first poem greets at last one who is "bone from my bones." It answers the "not good" of being alone (2:18).
settings.readers: For Israel the narrator draws the lesson at once (2:24): this is why a man leaves his father and mother and holds to his wife. Jesus quotes that line as God's plan for marriage (Matthew 19:4–6).
views: Many readers hear simple joy at finding a true partner.
Walter Brueggemann reads "bone and flesh" as a covenant formula of loyalty, like the tribes' words to David in 2 Samuel 5:1; Victor Hamilton makes the same link.

traditions.q: Does the order of creation in chapter 2 limit the roles of women in the church?
views: Man and woman are equal in dignity and both are fully God's image (Catechism 369–372). The Church ordains only men as priests because Christ chose men as his apostles, not because women are lesser, and John Paul II taught that the Church has no authority to change this (Ordinatio Sacerdotalis, 1994).

The Baptist Faith and Message (2000) says both men and women are gifted for service, but the office of pastor is limited to men, and Southern Baptists read 1 Timothy 2:12–13 as grounding this in the man being formed first. Other Baptist bodies, such as American Baptist Churches USA, ordain women, so Baptists are divided.

Reformed churches are divided. The Presbyterian Church in America and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church keep the offices of minister and elder for men, citing the order of 2:18–23; the Presbyterian Church (USA) and others have ordained women for decades, reading the helper of 2:18 as an equal partner.

Wesley allowed a few gifted women, such as Sarah Crosby and Mary Bosanquet, to preach. Most Methodist churches now ordain women, and American Methodists gave women full clergy rights in 1956, reading creation as a partnership.

Many Pentecostals point to Joel's promise that sons and daughters will prophesy, fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:17–18). The Assemblies of God has ordained women since 1935, though in practice women still lead fewer churches.

title: Where Are You?
sum: A shrewd snake asks the woman whether God really forbade every tree. She corrects him, adding "do not touch it." He tells her she will not die but will be like God. She sees the fruit is good, lovely and desirable for wisdom; she eats, and gives some to her husband, who is with her, and he eats. Their eyes open, and the first thing they see is their own nakedness.

They hide when the LORD God walks in the garden. He calls, "Where are you?" The man blames the woman and God; the woman blames the snake. God curses the snake and the ground, and announces pain, struggle and death, but also promises that the woman's offspring will strike the snake's head. He makes them clothes of skin, then sends them out of the garden, and cherubim guard the way to the tree of life.
readings: Read as history
The first couple really disobeyed God's single command, and sin and death entered the world through them, as Paul teaches (Romans 5:12–19). The snake was a real creature used by Satan.
Read as the story of every person
Many readers, Jewish and Christian, ancient and modern, see in Adam and Eve the pattern of every temptation: doubt about God's word, desire, grasping, shame, hiding and blame. "Adam" means "human."
Read as the founding of the human condition

Critical scholars read the chapter as an origin story explaining why snakes crawl, why childbirth hurts, why farming is hard, why we wear clothes, and why we die, told with deep insight into human nature.

views.L: A historical first sin by the first couple in a real garden. Physical death, for humans and animals, entered the world here, and the whole creation was cursed (Romans 8:20–22). Genesis 3:15 is the first promise of Christ.
views.O: A historical fall of the first humans or of humanity's representatives. Many old-earth readers hold that the death that came through sin was human (spiritual and physical), not the death of animals, which they see in the fossil record long before humans.
views.F: The fall is real, but told in symbolic images: a talking snake, magic-like trees, God walking in a garden-temple. Its point is that humans, made as God's images, grasped at being like God on their own terms, broke relationship with him and with each other, and lost access to life.
views.C: Most critical scholars read the story as wisdom-like reflection on maturity, knowledge and mortality. Some see a coming-of-age: gaining knowledge costs innocence. The snake is a snake; the identification with Satan comes much later, in Jewish and Christian writings.
views.J: Jewish tradition does not teach inherited guilt. The story shows the power of the evil inclination and the freedom to resist it. The rabbis linked God's question "Where are you?" (ayyekkah) with "How lonely" (eikhah) in Lamentations, so that Adam's exile foreshadows Israel's. God's clothing the couple is the model for clothing the naked (Talmud, Sotah 14a).

deep.b: The scene after the eating is built like a trial. God questions in reverse order of the sin (man, woman, snake) and then sentences in the order of the sin (snake, woman, man). The man is asked a question and answers with blame: "The woman! You set her at my side" (3:12). The woman blames the snake. The snake is not questioned. Each sentence touches the area of life that defines its hearer in that world: the snake's movement, the woman's childbearing and marriage, the man's farming. Only the snake and the ground are cursed.

deep.h: Original sin: how the churches and the synagogue read it
deep.b: Western churches follow Augustine. Lutheran, Reformed and many evangelical confessions speak of inherited guilt and a fallen nature. Catholic teaching calls original sin "contracted, not committed": a loss of original holiness and justice that is not a personal fault, leaving human nature wounded but not totally corrupted (Catechism 404–405), and Pius XII held that it comes from one first parent (Humani generis 37). Eastern Orthodox Christians speak of inherited mortality and corruption but not inherited guilt. Wesleyans add that God's grace goes ahead of every person, enabling response. Judaism teaches that people are born with competing inclinations and are responsible for their own sins (Ezekiel 18:20). Many modern theologians describe sin as a condition humans are born into, socially and personally, whatever one thinks of the history of Genesis 3.

deep.title: Gilgamesh and the snake
deep.b: At the end of the Epic of Gilgamesh, the hero finds a plant called "Old Man Grows Young" at the bottom of the sea. While he bathes in a pool, a snake smells it, takes it, and sheds its skin as it goes. Gilgamesh weeps: immortality is lost. Both stories link a snake with the loss of endless life, and both end with the hero going home to die. The differences are deep: in Genesis the loss comes through disobedience to God, not bad luck, and the story includes a promise.

deep.title: The first question and the last answer
deep.body: My own reading: God's first words to a human after the sin are a question, "Where are you?" (3:9), and the Bible's first question of all is the snake's twisting "Is it really true that God said...?" (3:1). Genesis 3 sets God's searching question against the snake's doubting one. Luke 19:10 ("the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost") reads like an answer to 3:9. The connection is a reading of the whole Bible, not something Genesis states.

echoes: Romans 5:12–21; Romans 8:20–22; Romans 16:20; 1 Corinthians 15:21–22; 2 Corinthians 11:3; 1 Timothy 2:13–14; Hebrews 2:14–15; 1 John 3:8; Revelation 12:9; Revelation 20:2; Revelation 22:2–3; Isaiah 65:25; Ezekiel 28:13–17; Ecclesiastes 3:20

settings.to: The snake, then the woman, then the man (Adam), in the garden
settings.when: After God has questioned each of them and each has passed the blame
settings.why: To pass sentence. The snake is cursed and will lose its war with the woman's offspring. The woman's bearing of children becomes painful, and her bond with her husband becomes a struggle. The ground is cursed, so the man's work becomes toil until he returns to dust. Only the snake and the ground are cursed, not the humans.
settings.readers: For Israel the words explained why life is the way it is: labor pains, hard farming, conflict between the sexes, and death. Israelite farmers on stony hill land knew the thorns and the sweat at first hand.
views: From Irenaeus on, many Christians read 3:15 as the first promise of Christ, the woman's offspring who crushes the serpent (compare Romans 16:20).
A story of how things are
Jewish readers and many scholars read 3:15 as the lasting hostility between humans and snakes, and the whole speech as an account of the hardships of life.
A broken order, not an ideal
Many readers stress that "he will rule over you" (3:16) describes what sin brings, not what God wants. Carol Meyers reads the verse against the heavy work of village women in early Israel.

settings.what: The LORD's decision to send the man out
settings.to: No one in the story; the narrator reports God's words
settings.when: After God has clothed the man and woman
settings.why: To decide that the man, who now knows good and evil, must not also take from the tree of life and live forever. So God sends him out of the garden and guards the way back with cherubim (3:23–24). The exile is also a mercy: an endless life in a fallen state is shut off.
settings.readers: For Israel the cherubim guarding the way to life appear again on the ark and the curtains of the tabernacle (Exodus 25:18–22; 26:31). The way back into God's presence was guarded there too, and opened only as God allowed.

traditions.q: What did Adam's sin pass on to his children: guilt, a damaged nature, or death?
views: Every person inherits a human nature deprived of the holiness Adam first had; this is called sin only in a special sense, "contracted, not committed" (Catechism 404–405). Baptism takes away original sin, but a pull toward sin remains, which the Council of Trent said is not itself sin.

We inherit death and a corrupted, weakened nature from Adam, and this leads each person into sin, but not Adam's personal guilt. Orthodox writers often read Romans 5:12 as saying that because of death all sinned.

The Augsburg Confession teaches that since the fall all are born without true fear of God or trust in him and with sinful desire, and that this inborn disease is truly sin that condemns. Unlike Trent, Lutherans hold that this desire is still sin after baptism, though God does not count it against the believer.

Adam stood as the head of the whole human race, so the guilt of his sin is counted to all his descendants and a corrupted nature is passed on (Westminster Confession 6.3). Every part of the person is affected, which is what Reformed churches mean by total depravity.

Wesley defended original sin strongly, yet taught that God's grace goes before every person and enables a response, so no one is left with sin alone. The Methodist Articles of Religion keep the doctrine while stressing this grace.

Baptists are divided. The Baptist Faith and Message (2000) says people inherit a nature and setting inclined toward sin and become guilty once they are capable of moral action, so many Baptists believe infants who die are saved; Calvinistic Baptists follow the 1689 Confession, which teaches inherited guilt.

traditions.q: Is Mary the woman whose offspring crushes the snake (3:15)?
views: The Latin Vulgate read "she will crush your head," and Catholic art shows Mary with her foot on the serpent. Modern Catholic Bibles read "he" or "they," but the Church still sees Mary, the new Eve, in the woman, and Pius IX cited this verse when he defined the Immaculate Conception in 1854 (Catechism 410–411; Lumen Gentium 55).

The offspring is Christ, and the fathers from Justin and Irenaeus on called Mary the new Eve, whose obedience undid Eve's disobedience. The Orthodox honor Mary as all-holy but do not accept the 1854 dogma of her Immaculate Conception.

Luther rejected the reading "she" and taught that the offspring who crushes the snake is Christ alone; Adam and Eve were saved by trusting this promise. Luther still honored Mary deeply as the mother of God.

Calvin read the offspring first as the human race in its long war with evil, led and won by Christ its head, and called the Marian reading a mistake built on a bad translation. The verse promises the gospel, not a role for Mary.

Most evangelicals read 3:15 as the first promise of the gospel, fulfilled when Christ was born of a woman and defeated Satan at the cross (Galatians 4:4; Romans 16:20). Mary is honored as a faithful believer, but she is not the subject of the verse.

title: Am I My Brother's Guard?
sum: Outside the garden, Eve gives birth to Cain and then Abel. Abel keeps flocks, Cain farms. Both bring gifts to the LORD; the LORD looks with favor on Abel's gift and not on Cain's. Cain burns with anger, and God warns him that sin is crouching at his door, wanting him, and he must rule it. Cain lures Abel out into the open country and kills him. When God asks where Abel is, Cain answers, "Am I my brother's guard?" Abel's blood cries from the ground. Cain is driven away to wander, but God sets a sign for him so that no one will kill him.

Cain's descendants build the first city and found herding, music and metalwork. The seventh of them, Lamech, takes two wives and boasts that he will be avenged "seventy and seven". The chapter closes with a new start: Eve bears Seth, "another offspring" in Abel's place, and in the days of Seth's son Enosh people begin to call on the name of the LORD.
readings: Read as history
The first family's second generation: a real murder, a real exile, and the first steps of civilization. Cain's wife was one of Adam's daughters (5:4). The family lines are records of real people.
Read as a story about anger and brothers

The chapter is a study of envy. God speaks to Cain before the murder, warns him, and offers him a choice. It begins the Bible's long series of rival brothers: Isaac and Ishmael, Jacob and Esau, Joseph and his brothers.
Read as the growth of civilization and violence
Critical and literary readers trace two things growing together: culture (cities, music, tools) and violence (from one murder to Lamech's boast). Human progress does not cure the human heart.

views.L: Cain and Abel were Adam and Eve's first sons. Cain married a sister; incest laws came later. The long ages and early arts are history. Abel's offering pleased God because it was by faith and from the best (Hebrews 11:4).
views.O: Most old-earth readers also read the chapter as history. Some suggest that the presence of other people (4:14, 17) shows that Adam and Eve were not the only humans of their time, or that a long time passed between the events.
views.F: Cain is the pattern of the sinner who refuses God's warning; the two lines, Cain's and Seth's, are the two ways of human life. The chapter is carefully built around "brother" (seven times) and sevens (sevenfold, seventy-sevenfold).
views.C: Most critical scholars think the Cain story once stood on its own, in a world already full of people, perhaps as the origin story of the Kenites, a clan of smiths. Cain's genealogy (4:17–24) and Seth's (5:1–32) look like two versions of one list.
views.J: The Mishnah reads "your brother's bloods" (4:10, Hebrew) as Abel and all his unborn descendants, and draws the lesson that one life is a whole world (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5). The Targums supply Cain and Abel's argument: whether there is justice and a judge. Some midrash reads Cain's words in 4:13 as repentance, and sees in his protection a sign that repentance has power.

deep.b: The text gives clues but no verdict. Abel brings "some of the firstborn of his flock and of their fat," the best; Cain brings "some of the fruit of the ground," with no mention of firstfruits. God looks at the person first, then the gift ("on Abel and his gift"). God's word to Cain (4:7) assumes Cain knows how to "do well." The New Testament speaks of Abel's faith and righteousness and of Cain's evil works (Hebrews 11:4; 1 John 3:12; Jude 11). The view that only animal sacrifices were acceptable is common in some Christian teaching, but the Law later accepts grain offerings, and both are called a minchah.

Herding and farming began in the Near East around 9000 to 8000 BC, cities around 4000 to 3500 BC (Uruk, called Erech in 10:10), bronze in the 3000s BC, and iron working became widespread after 1200 BC. Genesis 4 puts all of these in the first generations of humans. Young-earth readers take this as history compressed into a few generations; others see the list as a summary of the rise of culture, not a timeline.

Cain's name, Qayin, is also the name of the Kenites, a clan of smiths and nomads who lived among Israel. Moses' father-in-law belonged to them (Judges 1:16), Heber the Kenite pitched his tent apart (Judges 4:11), and Balaam puns on their name: "Kain will be burned" (Numbers 24:21–22). Many scholars think Israel heard the story of a wandering, protected Cain partly as the story of these neighbors.

deep.title: The voice and the face
deep.body: My own reading: chapter 4 is full of faces and voices. Cain's face "falls" (4:5–6), he fears being "hidden from your face" (4:14), and he leaves "from before the LORD" (literally "from the face of the LORD," 4:16). Meanwhile Abel never speaks, but his blood has a "voice" (4:10), and Lamech demands that his wives "listen to my voice" (4:23). The silent victim is heard by God; the boastful killer has to demand a hearing. This pattern is suggested by the Hebrew wording; I have not seen it laid out in a commentary, though many note the falling face.
deep.refs: Genesis 4:5–6; Genesis 4:10; Genesis 4:14; Genesis 4:16; Genesis 4:23; Hebrews 12:24

echoes: Matthew 5:21–24; Matthew 18:21–22; Matthew 23:35; Luke 11:51; Hebrews 11:4; Hebrews 12:24; 1 John 3:11–15; Jude 11; Exodus 20:13; Numbers 35:33; Joel 2:32; Romans 10:13

settings.to: Cain, angry and downcast because his gift was not accepted
settings.why: To warn Cain before he acts. Sin is crouching at the door like an animal and wants him, but he must rule over it. God speaks to the angry man as a free person who can still choose.
settings.readers: For Israel the words echo the struggle of 3:16 and teach that anger is a door, not a fate. The rabbis read "you must rule over it" as proof that a person can master the evil inclination.

settings.what: The questioning and sentence of Cain
settings.to: Cain, after he has killed his brother in the open country
settings.why: To call the murderer to account. Abel's blood cries out from the ground, so the ground will no longer yield to Cain, and he must wander. When Cain fears that anyone who finds him will kill him, God puts a sign on him and limits revenge.
settings.readers: For Israel, which knew the blood feud, God hears the blood of the victim and also restrains vengeance. Israel's later laws on murder and on places of refuge work with the same two concerns (Exodus 21:12–14; Numbers 35).

settings.by: Lamech, the seventh from Adam in Cain's line
settings.when: After his sons have founded herding, music and metalwork
settings.why: A boast in poetry. He has killed a man for wounding him, and he will be avenged seventy-seven times. God's limit on revenge for Cain (4:15) becomes a threat without limit.
settings.readers: For Israel, the song placed after the first city and the first tools of bronze and iron showed how fast skill and violence grow together. Jesus turns the number around when he tells Peter how often to forgive (Matthew 18:21–22).

title: And He Died
sum: "This is the book of the family history of Adam." Ten generations run from Adam to Noah, each with the same pattern: he lived so many years, fathered a son, lived so many more years and fathered other children, and he died. The repeated "and he died" makes the chapter a slow drumbeat of the sentence of 3:19.

Two entries break the pattern. Enoch, the seventh, "walked with God," and instead of dying "he was gone, for God took him." And Lamech, the ninth, names his son Noah, hoping that through him there will be relief from the cursed ground. The lifespans of nearly a thousand years, and the very different numbers in the Samaritan and Greek texts, have puzzled readers for two thousand years.
readings: Read as history
A real family tree from Adam to Noah. The ages are literal, and with chapter 11 they give a chronology from creation to Abraham. Long lives before the flood were real and declined afterward.
Read as a genealogy with a purpose

Ancient genealogies served to connect people, not always to count years. Ten generations, the seventh special, numbers built from meaningful patterns: the list links Adam to Noah and shows death reigning, with two signs of hope.
Read beside the Babylonian king lists
Critical scholars compare the Sumerian King List and Berossus, which list long-lived rulers before the flood. Genesis keeps the form but humanizes it: fathers, not kings, and every one of them dies.

views.L: The ages are exact. Adding them gives 1,656 years from creation to the flood (Masoretic Text). Long lives may reflect a better pre-flood world and a fresh human genome. The lists are complete, since each father's age at the next son's birth is given.
views.O: Many old-earth evangelicals follow William Henry Green (1890): Hebrew genealogies can skip generations, "fathered" can mean "was the ancestor of," and Scripture never totals these numbers, so they cannot date creation. The ages are taken as real by some and as honorific by others.
views.F: The chapter's shape matters more than its arithmetic: ten generations, a refrain of death, the seventh man taken by God, the tenth man saving the world. The numbers may be symbolic, as Cassuto argued from their structure in multiples of five and seven.
views.C: Most critical scholars assign the chapter to the Priestly source and see it as a reworking of the same old list found in 4:17–18. The numbers in the three textual traditions differ because scribes revised them systematically; none can simply be read as history.
views.J: The Mishnah notes ten generations from Adam to Noah, "to show how patient God is, for every one of them provoked him" (Avot 5:2). Methuselah's death in the flood year was read as God waiting until the righteous man died. Ben Azzai called 5:1 the greatest principle in the Torah, because all humans share one ancestor.

deep.b: The Masoretic Text, the Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint give different ages at fatherhood. The Septuagint adds 100 years to most fathers' ages (and subtracts 100 from their remaining years, so lifespans match). The Samaritan lowers Jared's, Methuselah's and Lamech's numbers so that all three die in the year of the flood. The result: 1,656 years from creation to the flood in the Hebrew, 1,307 in the Samaritan, and 2,242 in most Greek manuscripts (2,262 if the minority reading 187 for Methuselah is followed). Ralph Klein and Ronald Hendel argue that all three reworked an earlier set of numbers; some evangelical scholars have argued that the Septuagint numbers are original (Henry B. Smith). The Plain English follows the Masoretic Text and shows the others as variants.

Adam to Noah is ten generations, and Shem to Abram (11:10–26) is ten more (counting the Masoretic list). The Sumerian and Babylonian lists also name about ten figures before the flood. Matthew arranges Jesus' ancestors in three sets of fourteen, leaving out several kings to do it (Matthew 1:1–17), which shows that biblical genealogies can be shaped for a purpose.

deep.title: The Sumerian King List
deep.b: The list opens: "After kingship descended from heaven, kingship was in Eridu. In Eridu, Alulim became king; he ruled for 28,800 years." Eight kings in five cities reign 241,200 years, "then the flood swept over. After the flood swept over, kingship descended from heaven" again, to Kish, where reigns are still long but shrink over time. Berossus, a Babylonian priest writing in Greek about 290 BC, has ten kings before the flood, the last being Xisuthros, the flood hero. Verdict: the shape is similar to Genesis 5 and 11 (a list before the flood, shorter lives after), but the scale, the purpose and the theology are very different.

echoes: 1 Chronicles 1:1–4; Luke 3:36–38; Hebrews 11:5–6; Jude 14–15; Psalm 90:10; Romans 5:12–14; 2 Kings 2:11

title: The Earth Was Full of Violence
sum: As humans multiply, "the sons of God" take wives from the daughters of humankind, and the Nephilim are on the earth, the heroes of old. The LORD limits human days to 120 years. Then he sees how great human evil is: every plan of the human heart is evil all day long. The LORD is sorry he made humankind, and it pains him to the heart. He decides to wipe them out. "But Noah found favor in the LORD's eyes."

Noah is righteous, blameless in his generation, and walks with God. God tells him that the earth is ruined and full of violence, and that he will ruin it with a flood. Noah is to build an ark of gopher wood, three decks high, and bring his family and two of every kind of animal. God promises to set up his covenant with him. Noah does everything God commands.
readings: Read as history

Real angels or real men took wives; human wickedness grew; God judged the world by a historical flood and saved Noah's family. Jesus and Peter refer to the days of Noah as history (Matthew 24:37–39; 2 Peter 2:5).
Read as theology

The chapter shows God's heart: grief, not cold anger, over a world ruined by violence, and grace that chooses one man to begin again. The language of ruin (shachat) shows judgment as God completing what people had already done.
Read with ancient myth
Critical scholars read 6:1–4 as a fragment of a myth about gods and women and their giant children, like the Greek Titans, placed here to show the world spinning out of order before the flood.

views.L: The sons of God were fallen angels (or, for many, the line of Seth); the Nephilim were giants; 120 years was the time left before the flood. The ark was a real ship of the stated size, able to carry the animal kinds.
views.O: Old-earth readers who hold a regional flood take the ark as real and large but carrying only the animals of the region. The 120 years and the sons of God are read in the same range of ways as by other traditional readers.
views.F: 6:1–8 shows the boundary between heaven and earth broken from both sides, and the human heart "shaping" evil as God once shaped man. The ark, like the tabernacle later, is a God-designed structure built by obedience, a small world kept safe in God's care.
views.C: Most critical scholars see two flood sources woven together, the Yahwist (6:5–8) and the Priestly (6:9–22), and 6:1–4 as an old myth fragment. The story belongs with the Mesopotamian flood tradition, recast to teach one God's moral judgment.
views.J: The rabbis debated whether Noah was righteous only by his generation's low standard or would have been greater in a better one (Sanhedrin 108a). Targum Onkelos reads the sons of God as "sons of the great ones," rulers. The 120 years were the time Noah spent building, so people would ask him what he was doing and repent (Rashi; Genesis Rabbah 30:7).

deep.h: Who were the sons of God? The three views
deep.b: Angels is the oldest attested view (1 Enoch 6–11; Jubilees 5:1; Philo; Josephus; most early Christian writers), and many modern scholars, critical and conservative, hold it on the grounds that "sons of God" means divine beings in Job 1:6 and 38:7. Jude 6–7 and 2 Peter 2:4–5 seem to assume it. Sethites (Julius Africanus, Augustine, Chrysostom, Luther, Calvin) avoids the difficulty of angels marrying (Matthew 22:30) and fits the contrast of the two lines in chapters 4–5. Rulers (the Targums, Genesis Rabbah, many medieval Jewish commentators, and Meredith Kline) takes the phrase as a title of kings, who in the ancient world could be called sons of a god, taking harems by force. The passage is short and unusual, and certainty is not possible.

The ark's dimensions, 300 by 50 by 30 cubits, give a length-to-width ratio of 6 to 1, close to many modern cargo ships. The largest known wooden ships of the 1800s and early 1900s, such as the schooner Wyoming (about 450 feet overall), needed iron bracing and still leaked badly. Young-earth writers answer that the ark did not need to sail, only to float. The reconstruction at the Ark Encounter in Kentucky (2016) was built at full size using a long cubit of about 20.4 inches.

deep.title: Shaping and grieving
deep.body: My own reading of the verbs: in 2:7 God yatsar, "shaped," the man, and in 6:5 humans' hearts produce a yetser, a "shaping," of evil. In 3:16–17 God announces itsavon, "pain," for humans; in 6:6 God himself is pained (vayyit'atsev). Genesis seems to say that the creature has turned the Creator's own craft against him, and that the pain announced to humans has come back to God. The verbal links are well known to commentators; the suggestion that they are meant as a pair is mine.

echoes: Job 1:6; Job 38:7; Numbers 13:33; 1 Samuel 15:11; 1 Samuel 15:29; Ezekiel 14:14; Matthew 24:37–39; Luke 17:26–27; Hebrews 11:7; 1 Peter 3:19–20; 2 Peter 2:4–5; Jude 6–7

settings.what: The LORD's decision to wipe out humankind
settings.to: No one in the story; the narrator lets the readers overhear God's grief
settings.when: When human evil has grown great on the earth
settings.why: To decide on the flood. Every plan of the human heart is evil all day long, and the LORD is sorry he made humankind, pained to his heart. The judgment comes from grief, not anger alone. Noah alone finds favor (6:8).
settings.readers: For Israel this was a God who feels the wrong done to his world. Ancient flood stories blamed the gods' annoyance at human noise; here the cause is moral evil. The same words about the human heart return when God promises never to do it again (8:21).

settings.to: Noah, the one righteous man of his generation
settings.when: When the earth is full of violence and God has decided on the flood
settings.why: To warn Noah of the flood, tell him how to build the ark, and promise him a covenant. The careful measurements show God planning rescue as carefully as judgment.
settings.readers: For Israel the ark coated with pitch had an echo in the basket of the baby Moses, the same Hebrew word, tevah (Exodus 2:3). A holy structure built exactly as God commanded also looks ahead to the tabernacle (Exodus 25–40).
views: Literal readers take the speech as God's plan for a flood over the whole earth.

Old-earth readers often think of a great regional flood. Critical scholars compare the Mesopotamian flood stories, where one god secretly warns one man. They see Genesis answering them with a God who judges violence and openly saves the righteous.

title: The Windows of the Sky
sum: The LORD tells Noah to go into the ark with his household, taking seven pairs of every clean animal and bird and one pair of the others, because in seven days the rain will come. Noah, now 600 years old, goes in with his wife, his sons and their wives, and the animals come two by two. On the seventeenth day of the second month the springs of the great deep burst open and the windows of the sky open. The LORD shuts the door behind them.

Rain falls for forty days and nights. The waters rise and lift the ark, then cover the high mountains by fifteen cubits. Everything on dry land with the breath of life dies. Only Noah and those with him in the ark are left, and the waters rule over the earth for 150 days.
readings: Read as history
A real flood, dated to the day in Noah's life, covering the whole earth or at least the whole human world, in which all humans and land animals outside the ark died.
Read as creation undone
The waters God separated on days two and three rush back together; the earth returns toward the formless deep of 1:2. The flood is uncreation, so that God can make the world again with Noah.
Read as two sources woven together

Critical scholars point to doublets: two of each animal or seven of the clean; forty days or 150; "God" and "the LORD." They separate a Yahwist and a Priestly account. Others argue that the repetitions are deliberate emphasis in a single narrative.

views.L: A worldwide flood that covered every mountain, laid down most fossil-bearing rock layers, and reshaped the continents (catastrophic plate tectonics, Baumgardner and others). The ark carried two of each land-animal kind, perhaps a few thousand animals.
views.O: A huge but regional flood that destroyed the human world of the time in Mesopotamia (Hugh Ross; Davis Young; earlier, John Pye Smith). "All the high mountains under the whole sky" describes what the observers saw, as "all the earth" in 41:57 means the lands around Egypt.
views.F: The account uses the language of 1:2–10 in reverse to present the flood as a cosmic judgment and a return to chaos, from which God brings a new creation. The numbers form a careful mirror pattern (Wenham). Whatever its extent, its message is God's judgment on violence and his rescue.
views.C: Most critical scholars read the flood as a Mesopotamian tradition, perhaps rooted in memories of river floods, transformed into a story of one God's moral judgment. Geologists regard it as consensus that no worldwide flood happened in human history.
views.J: The rabbis said the seven days of 7:10 were mourning for Methuselah (Sanhedrin 108b). They debated whether the second month was in autumn or spring (Rosh Hashanah 11b). Rashi notes that Noah entered the ark only when the waters forced him (7:7), since he "believed and did not believe" that the flood would come.

deep.b: For a global flood: the language is universal ("all," "under the whole sky"); the waters stand above the mountains for months; an ark would be unnecessary for a local flood, since Noah could have moved; God promises never again to send such a flood, but local floods still happen; Jesus and Peter compare it to a universal judgment (Luke 17:27; 2 Peter 3:6). For a regional flood: Hebrew erets also means "land" and kol often means "very many" (41:57; Deuteronomy 2:25); the point of view is the survivors'; geology shows no single worldwide flood layer, and many fossils and rock layers took long ages to form; the animals' distribution today (for example, kangaroos in Australia) is hard to explain from one ark. For a non-historical story: the parallels with Mesopotamian flood stories and the theological shape of the narrative suggest a traditional story retold for its meaning.

In 1929 Leonard Woolley found a layer of clean, water-laid clay about 8 to 11 feet thick at Ur and announced that he had found the flood. Later digs found flood layers at Kish, Shuruppak (the city of the Babylonian flood hero) and Uruk, but from different periods, and some sites close to Ur show none. Most archaeologists now think these were local river floods. William Ryan and Walter Pitman proposed in 1998 that the Black Sea flooded catastrophically about 5600 BC; geologists still debate how fast and how large that event was.

deep.title: The flood in Atrahasis
deep.b: In Atrahasis (Old Babylonian, about 1700 BC), the gods create humans to do their work; humans multiply and make so much noise that the god Enlil cannot sleep. After plague, drought and famine fail, the gods send a flood. The wise god Enki warns Atrahasis through a reed wall to build a boat. The storm lasts seven days; the gods, without human offerings, grow hungry and thirsty and regret the flood. Afterward the gods limit human numbers by barrenness and infant death. Verdict: Genesis shares the outline but reverses the reason (violence, not noise), the character of God (one, just and grieved, not quarreling), and the ending (a blessing to fill the earth).

echoes: Matthew 24:38–39; Luke 17:26–27; Hebrews 11:7; 1 Peter 3:20–21; 2 Peter 2:5; 2 Peter 3:5–7; Isaiah 54:9; Psalm 29:10; Exodus 24:18; Matthew 4:2

settings.why: To call Noah in, with seven pairs of every clean animal and one pair of the others, and to set the day.
settings.readers: For Israel the mention of clean animals assumed its own laws on food and sacrifice (Leviticus 11). It also prepared for Noah's offering in 8:20, so Noah acts as a priest.
views: Many critical scholars read 7:1–4 (J, seven pairs of clean animals) and 6:19–20 (P, two of each kind) as two versions woven together.
Others (Cassuto, Wenham) read 7:1–4 as a fuller second command once the ark is built.

title: God Remembered Noah
sum: "God remembered Noah." He sends a wind over the earth, the springs of the deep and the windows of the sky are closed, and the waters begin to go down. In the seventh month the ark comes to rest on the mountains of Ararat; in the tenth month the mountain tops appear. Noah sends out a raven, which goes back and forth, then a dove three times: the first comes back, the second brings a fresh olive leaf, the third does not return.

In Noah's 601st year the ground is dry, and God tells Noah to come out with everyone and every creature, to swarm, be fruitful and multiply. Noah builds an altar and offers burnt offerings of every clean animal and bird. The LORD smells the soothing smell and says in his heart that he will not curse the ground any more because of humankind, though "what the human heart shapes is evil from youth on." While the earth lasts, seed time and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night will not stop.
readings: Read as history
The flood ends on a stated calendar; the ark lands in the mountains of Urartu (eastern Turkey and Armenia); Noah's family and the animals leave to repopulate the earth.
Read as new creation

A wind (ruach) over the waters, dry land appearing, birds and animals sent out to multiply, a blessing to be fruitful: chapter 8 retells Genesis 1. The turning point of the whole flood story is 8:1, "God remembered."
Read beside Gilgamesh

The closest parallel in all ancient literature: the boat lands on a mountain, the hero sends out birds, he offers sacrifice, and the gods smell the sweet savor. Genesis tells the same scene with a single God who makes a lasting promise.

views.L: By the Hebrew dates the flood lasted just over a year (from 2/17 of year 600 to 2/27 of year 601); the Greek dates make it exactly one year. The ark rested on a real peak in the Ararat range. Some young-earth writers link the receding waters to the rise of mountains and the carving of canyons.
views.O: Regional-flood readers place the ark's landing in the foothills of the Ararat region, north of Mesopotamia. The "mountains" of 8:4 is plural, a range, not the single modern Mount Ararat (named later).
views.F: The structure is a mirror (a chiasm) whose center is 8:1, "God remembered Noah" (Wenham). Everything before rises toward judgment, everything after falls toward rescue. God's promise in 8:21–22 is grace in spite of the human heart, not because of it.
views.C: Critical scholars assign the dated calendar entries to the Priestly source and the birds and sacrifice to the Yahwist, whose story stands closest to Gilgamesh XI. Nearly all scholars agree that Genesis and Gilgamesh XI share a tradition; most critical scholars think Genesis depends on it, directly or indirectly, while many conservatives think both descend from a common memory.
views.J: The rabbis noted that "God remembered" uses the name for God's justice (Elohim), and taught that God's justice itself turned to mercy (Genesis Rabbah 33:3, cited by Rashi). 8:22 was read as a promise of the fixed order of nature, and 8:21 ("evil from youth on") as the basis of the teaching on the evil inclination, the yetser ha-ra.

deep.b: Ararat is the Hebrew form of Urartu, a kingdom around Lake Van in the 800s to 600s BC (see 2 Kings 19:37; Jeremiah 51:27). Genesis says "the mountains of Ararat," a region. The Babylonian story puts the landing on Mount Nimush (or Nisir), and Syriac and Islamic tradition point to Mount Judi (Qardu) in southeastern Turkey. The 16,854-foot peak now called Mount Ararat received that name in the Middle Ages. Many expeditions have searched it for the ark; no find has been confirmed.

deep.title: Gilgamesh, Tablet XI
deep.b: Utnapishtim tells Gilgamesh: "On Mount Nimush the boat ran aground... When the seventh day arrived, I brought out a dove and set it free. The dove went off and came back; no resting place appeared, so it turned around. I brought out a swallow... I brought out a raven and set it free; the raven went off, saw the waters receding, ate, circled, and did not turn back." He offers a sacrifice: "The gods smelled the savor, the gods smelled the sweet savor, the gods gathered like flies over the offering." Verdict: the closest parallel known. The differences are just as striking: the order of birds, the hungry gods crowding round, and the lack of any promise for the earth's future (instead, Utnapishtim is made immortal).

deep.title: The raven that did not come back
deep.body: My own observation: the raven "went out, going and coming back" (8:7), never quite leaving and never quite coming home. It is the creature of the old world, content with what floats on the waters. The dove looks for a resting place, the same word (manoach) as Noah's name sounds like (noach, "rest"). Only when the dove finds rest does Noah. Rabbinic and patristic writers make much of the raven and dove; the link to Noah's name through manoach is a wordplay noted by some commentators, but the full reading is my own.

echoes: Exodus 2:24; Exodus 14:21; 1 Samuel 1:19; Psalm 8:4; Isaiah 54:9–10; Jeremiah 33:20–25; Matthew 3:16; Ephesians 5:2; Philippians 4:18; Leviticus 1:9

settings.what: The LORD's promise in his heart
settings.to: No one in the story: God says it "in his heart," and the narrator lets the readers overhear it
settings.when: After Noah's burnt offering on leaving the ark
settings.why: To promise that God will not curse the ground again or strike every living thing, even though the human heart is still bent toward evil from youth. Seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter will not stop. The same fact about the human heart that caused the flood (6:5) is now the reason for God's patience.
settings.readers: For Israel, farmers who lived by rain and seasons, this was the ground of their trust in the yearly cycle. The prophet Jeremiah later made the fixed order of day and night a pledge of God's covenant with Israel (Jeremiah 33:20–21).

title: My Bow in the Clouds
sum: God blesses Noah and his sons: be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth. Animals will now fear humans, and every living thing that moves may be food, but not flesh with its life-blood still in it. Whoever spills a human's blood, by a human his blood will be spilled, for God made humans in his image. Then God makes a covenant with Noah, his descendants and every living creature: never again will a flood destroy the earth. The sign is his bow in the clouds.

Noah, a man of the soil, plants a vineyard, drinks wine, and lies uncovered in his tent. Ham, Canaan's father, sees his father's nakedness and tells his brothers; Shem and Japheth walk in backwards and cover him. When Noah wakes, he curses Canaan to be a slave to his brothers and blesses Shem and Japheth. Noah lives 350 years after the flood and dies at 950.
readings: Read as history
The renewed blessing, the first law against murder, the rainbow covenant and the story of Noah's drunkenness are records of real events after the flood.
Read as the charter of a new world

Chapter 9 restates Genesis 1 for a fallen world: the same blessing, but now with fear, meat, death penalty and a covenant with all life. The Noahic covenant is the Bible's first, unconditional and universal.
Read as Israel's story about Canaan

Critical readers see 9:20–27 as explaining why Israel ruled the Canaanites: their ancestor was cursed. The curse falls on Canaan, not on Ham, which shows the story's interest in Israel's neighbors, not in Africa.

views.L: Rainbows began after the flood, either because pre-flood conditions were different or because God gave an existing sight a new meaning. Noah's drunkenness and the curse are history. The curse on Canaan was fulfilled in Israel's conquest.
views.O: Most old-earth readers hold that rainbows existed before the flood (they follow from light and water drops) and that God gave the bow a new meaning as a sign, as he later made circumcision a sign.
views.F: The bow (qeshet) is a war bow hung in the sky: God laying down his weapon, pointed away from the earth. The covenant with all living creatures is the basis of the hope that God will not abandon his world.
views.C: Critical scholars assign the covenant (9:1–17) to the Priestly source, with circumcision (17) and Sabbath (Exodus 31) as covenant signs; the vineyard story is Yahwist. The curse on Canaan justifies Israel's claims to the land.
views.J: The rabbis derived from 9:1–7 the seven Noahide laws binding all humankind (against idolatry, blasphemy, murder, sexual sin, theft, eating flesh from a living animal, and for courts of justice; Sanhedrin 56a). A Gentile who keeps them has a share in the world to come (Tosefta Sanhedrin 13:2; Maimonides). Some midrash says Ham castrated or abused Noah (Sanhedrin 70a).

deep.h: The "curse of Ham" and its misuse
deep.b: Noah curses Canaan, not Ham (9:25). Even so, from the medieval period onward some Jewish, Christian and Muslim writers claimed that Ham was cursed with black skin and slavery, and this teaching was used in the Atlantic slave trade and in American and South African racial laws. The text says nothing about skin, and Ham's descendants in chapter 10 include peoples of many regions. Christian scholars and churches of all kinds now reject the racial reading as a misuse of the text. David Goldenberg's study The Curse of Ham (2003) traces the history of the idea.

The Noahide laws gave rabbinic Judaism a way to describe righteous Gentiles without requiring conversion: the Torah's 613 commandments are for Israel, the seven laws for everyone. Acts 15:20, 29 gives Gentile believers a short list of rules (idols, sexual sin, strangled animals, blood) that many scholars connect with this same idea or with Leviticus 17–18.

deep.title: A covenant with the animals
deep.body: My own emphasis: the word "covenant" appears seven times in 9:8–17, and again and again the other party is "every living creature." Before God makes any covenant with Abraham or Israel, his first covenant is with the whole earth and its animals. That shapes how I read later promises of a renewed creation (Hosea 2:18; Romans 8:19–22): the animals were in the covenant from the start. This is not an unusual reading, but the stress is mine.

echoes: Genesis 1:28; Genesis 1:29–30; Leviticus 17:10–14; Exodus 21:12; Romans 13:4; Acts 15:20; Isaiah 54:9; Ezekiel 1:28; Revelation 4:3; Revelation 10:1; Hosea 2:18

settings.what: The blessing and laws for Noah's sons
settings.to: Noah and his sons, and through them all humankind after the flood
settings.when: As they come out of the ark into a new world
settings.why: To renew the blessing of 1:28, with new rules for a world that is still violent. Animals may now be eaten, but not with their lifeblood. Murder must be paid for with the murderer's life, because humans bear God's image. These laws bind every human being, not only Israel. They answer the problem of violence that brought the flood: life, even animal life, belongs to God.
settings.readers: For Israel the ban on blood was a law it kept itself (Leviticus 17:10–14), now shown to be older than Sinai. Jewish tradition built on these verses the laws of the children of Noah, which any non-Jew must keep to be righteous. The apostles asked Gentile believers to avoid blood (Acts 15:20).
views: The rabbis derive part of the seven Noahide laws from these verses, and Maimonides sets them out as binding on all peoples (Laws of Kings 9:1).
Many critical scholars assign the passage to the Priestly source (P) and read it as the base of the ban on blood that Israel kept.

settings.to: Noah and his sons, their offspring after them, and every living creature that came out of the ark
settings.when: After the blessing, before Noah's sons spread out
settings.why: To make the first covenant in the Bible: an oath with no conditions that God will never again destroy all flesh by a flood. The sign is his bow in the clouds, and it reminds God, not humans. The covenant is with the whole earth.
settings.readers: For Israel its own covenants stood inside this wider promise to all life. In exile, Isaiah 54:9–10 used this oath to promise that God's anger with them would also end.
views: Many interpreters see the rainbow as God's battle bow hung up, pointed away from the earth.
Others read it simply as the rainbow, made into a sign.

settings.what: Noah's poem of curse and blessing
settings.to: His sons Shem, Ham and Japheth; the curse falls on Ham's son Canaan
settings.when: When Noah wakes from his wine and learns what Ham did
settings.why: To curse Canaan to be a slave to his brothers, to bless the God of Shem, and to pray that Japheth will live in Shem's tents. The words point beyond the family to nations. The text curses Canaan only.
settings.readers: For Israel, descended from Shem, the old poem explained why Canaan's peoples, whose land Israel would take, would serve them. Its later use to defend the enslavement of Africans as "sons of Ham" has no ground in the passage.
views: Many read Ham's sin as staring at and mocking his father's shame.
Some ancient and modern readers (Bergsma and Hahn) read "saw the nakedness" as a sexual act, which would explain why Ham's son is cursed.

traditions.q: Does 9:6 require governments to put murderers to death today?
views: The Church long accepted the death penalty, but in 2018 Pope Francis revised the Catechism to call it inadmissible, an attack on the dignity of the person, which modern prisons make unnecessary (Catechism 2267). Some Catholic thinkers have argued this is a change in judgment, not in doctrine.

Calvin and the Reformed tradition read 9:6 as a law for all nations given before Moses, giving rulers the sword to punish murder (Romans 13:4). Reformed churches today are divided: some hold this view, while the Presbyterian Church (USA) and the church before it have opposed the death penalty since 1959.

Many Baptists hold that 9:6 still gives the state the right to execute murderers, and the Southern Baptist Convention endorsed the death penalty in a 2000 resolution. Other Baptists oppose it, so practice is divided.

Mennonite and Brethren churches have long opposed the death penalty, holding that Christ calls his followers to give up killing and that God wants even murderers to repent. They hold that Christ's call to love enemies and not repay evil (Matthew 5:38–44) governs how Christians apply 9:6.
The United Methodist Church has opposed the death penalty since 1956, holding that no one is beyond God's redemption.

title: The Families of the Nations
sum: "This is the family history of Noah's sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth." Seventy names follow. The sons of Japheth spread over the coastlands to the north and west. The sons of Ham include Cush, Egypt, Put and Canaan; among them Nimrod, a mighty hunter, founds kingdoms in Babel and Assyria, including Nineveh. Canaan's sons settle from Sidon to Gaza.

The sons of Shem include Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud and Aram, and through Eber come Peleg, "for in his days the earth was split up," and Joktan's many sons in Arabia. Each section ends with the same formula: by their clans, their languages, their lands and their nations. "From them the nations parted and spread over the earth after the flood."
readings: Read as history
A real record of how Noah's grandsons gave rise to the peoples of the ancient world, many of whose names (Egypt, Canaan, Assyria, Elam) survive in history.
Read as a map of the world
The Table of Nations is unique in the ancient world: every known people, Israel's enemies included, placed in one family under God. Israel itself is not even named; it is one of many.
Read as ancient ethnography

Critical scholars see a combination of lists from different periods, ordered sometimes by descent, sometimes by geography, language or politics (Canaan is placed with Ham, though Canaanite was close to Hebrew).

views.L: All present nations descend from Noah's three sons, roughly Europe and northern Asia from Japheth, Africa and Canaan from Ham, the Middle East from Shem. The division in Peleg's days was the language split at Babel (some say continental drift).
views.O: Old-earth and regional-flood readers often take the table as describing the nations known to Israel, not all humanity, which fits a flood that destroyed the human world of the region.
views.F: Seventy nations (counted in the Masoretic Text) match the seventy of Jacob's family (46:27; Deuteronomy 32:8). The table puts the blessing of 9:1 into action and sets the stage for Abraham, through whom "all the families of the earth" will be blessed (12:3).
views.C: The table mixes Priestly and Yahwist material and reflects the world of the first millennium BC: the Medes (Madai), the Ionian Greeks (Javan), the Scythians (Ashkenaz) and Cimmerians (Gomer). This is the consensus basis for dating its final form no earlier than about 800 to 600 BC.
views.J: The seventy nations became a fixed idea in Jewish thought: seventy languages, seventy angels over the nations, seventy bulls offered at the Feast of Booths for the nations (Sukkah 55b). Nimrod became the arch-rebel who built Babel and threw Abraham into a furnace (Genesis Rabbah 38:13; Pesachim 118a).

deep.b: Nimrod is the first "hero" and the first king the Bible names, ruling in Babylonia and then Assyria (10:8–12; Micah 5:6 calls Assyria "the land of Nimrod"). No Mesopotamian king of that name is known; the proposed identifications are weighed in the note at 10:8. Later Jewish and Christian tradition made him the builder of Babel and a rebel against God (see the note at 10:9), though Genesis 11 never names him.

The Table of Nations is the oldest surviving attempt to map all known peoples into one family. Many names are known from outside the Bible: Gomer = the Gimirrai (Cimmerians), Madai = the Medes, Javan = the Ionians, Ashkenaz = the Ishkuza (Scythians), Cush = Nubia, Mizraim = Egypt, Asshur = Assyria, Elam = southwestern Iran, Aram = the Arameans of Syria. The count of seventy is in the Masoretic Text; the Septuagint, which adds Cainan and Elisa, has 72.

deep.title: Before Babel, or after it?
deep.body: My own note on order: chapter 10 already says the nations had their own "languages" (10:5, 20, 31), but chapter 11 begins with the whole earth speaking one language. So the table is not in time order; it gives the result first, then tells how it came about. Genesis does this elsewhere too (1:1–2:3 then 2:4–25). I find this a useful reminder that biblical narrative is often arranged by topic, which bears on how strictly to read the days and genealogies as sequences. Many commentators note the order; how far to press it is my own judgment.

echoes: 1 Chronicles 1:4–23; Deuteronomy 32:8; Acts 17:26; Acts 2:5–11; Ezekiel 38:2–6; Micah 5:6; Luke 10:1; Revelation 7:9

title: A Name for Ourselves
sum: The whole earth has one language. Moving east, people settle in the plain of Shinar and say, "Come on, let's mold bricks... Come on, let's build ourselves a city, and a tower with its head in the heavens. We will win a name for ourselves, and not be scattered across the face of all the earth." The LORD comes down to see the city, mixes up their language, and scatters them. The place is called Babel, because there the LORD mixed up (balal) the speech of all the earth.

The family history of Shem follows: ten generations, with lifespans falling sharply though not evenly, down to Terah. Terah fathers Abram, Nahor and Haran. Haran dies in Ur of the Chaldeans; Abram marries Sarai, who is barren; and Terah takes Abram, Sarai and his grandson Lot to go to Canaan, but they settle in Haran, where Terah dies.
readings: Read as history
A real tower at a real Babel, a real confusion of languages as the origin of the world's language families, and a real genealogy from Shem to Abraham, about 2000 BC.
Read as the climax of chapters 1–11

Humans try to reach heaven and make their own name; God comes down. The next chapter answers with God's own plan: "I will bless you and make your name great" (12:2). Babel leads to Abraham, and Pentecost (Acts 2) reverses Babel.
Read against Babylon
Critical scholars read the story as a satire on Babylon, its ziggurats, its proud name (Bab-ilu, "gate of the god"), and its claim to be the center of the world, mocked as balal, confusion.

views.L: Babel was a real event a few generations after the flood, explaining the origin of languages. Adding the ages in 11:10–26 (Masoretic Text) puts the flood 292 years before Abram's birth, so Noah is still alive when Abram is born, and Shem outlives Abraham.
views.O: The genealogy is selective (Luke 3:36 includes Cainan, absent from the Hebrew), so it cannot fix the date of the flood or Babel. The language confusion may describe a regional event among Noah's descendants, not the origin of all human languages.
views.F: The story is a tightly built reversal: "come, let us build" answered by "come, let us go down"; their wish to avoid scattering ends in scattering. God has to "come down" to see their tower that "reaches heaven," a gentle joke at its smallness.
views.C: The tower is a Babylonian ziggurat; Etemenanki, the great temple tower of Marduk in Babylon, is often suggested. Linguists regard it as consensus that languages diversified gradually over tens of thousands of years, not in one event.
views.J: The rabbis taught that the builders mourned when a brick fell but not when a man fell, and that they wanted to make war on heaven (Genesis Rabbah 38; Sanhedrin 109a; Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 24). Abram, born in Ur, was said to have broken his father Terah's idols (Genesis Rabbah 38:13).

deep.b: Mesopotamian cities had stepped temple towers called ziggurats, built of mud brick with baked brick facing and bitumen mortar, as 11:3 describes. Babylon's Etemenanki, "house of the foundation of heaven and earth," rose about 300 feet in seven stages and was rebuilt by Nebuchadnezzar II (about 600 BC), who wrote that he raised its top "to rival the heavens." The Enuma Elish says the gods built Babylon and its temple Esagila for Marduk, "lifting its head high." A tower "with its head in the heavens" uses language Babylonian kings used of their own temples.

deep.title: Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta
deep.b: A Sumerian epic (copies from about 2000 to 1700 BC) contains a passage called "the spell of Nudimmud": once "the whole universe, the people in unison, to Enlil in one tongue gave praise," until the god Enki "changed the speech in their mouths, brought contention into it." Scholars debate whether the passage looks back to a confusion of languages or forward to a hoped-for unity. Verdict: the only known ancient parallel to a single original language changed by a god, but there is no tower and no judgment on pride.
l: Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta
Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta

deep.b: Adding the Masoretic ages gives 292 years from the flood to Abram's birth and 1,948 years from creation to Abram (the traditional Jewish date, 1948 AM). The Samaritan Pentateuch gives 942 years for this stretch (2,249 years from creation), and the Septuagint, with its extra generation of Cainan, 1,072 (3,314 years from creation if Methuselah fathered Lamech at 167, or 3,334 with the reading 187). These totals follow from the numbers in the variants at 5:3 and 11:12. Archaeology places Ur's prosperity under its third dynasty about 2100 to 2000 BC.

deep.title: Babel, Abram and Pentecost
deep.body: My own reading of the three scenes together: at Babel people gather to make a name and are scattered; in 12:1–3 God scatters one man ("go from your land") and promises to make his name great; at Pentecost (Acts 2) God gathers people from every nation and each hears in his own language. The answer to Babel is not the return of one language but understanding across many. The link of Babel and Pentecost is ancient (it is in the church fathers); the observation that Pentecost keeps the many languages is often made, and the three-part pattern is how I see it.

echoes: Genesis 12:1–3; Acts 2:1–13; Zephaniah 3:9; Isaiah 14:13–14; Jeremiah 51:53; Daniel 4:30; Revelation 17–18; Luke 3:34–36; Acts 7:2–4; Joshua 24:2; Hebrews 11:8

settings.by: The LORD, speaking as "us," perhaps with his heavenly court
settings.to: No one in the story; the narrator reports God's words
settings.when: When the LORD comes down to see the city and the tower
settings.why: To mix up the builders' language and stop the project, so that humankind cannot unite to make a name for itself against God. The scattering follows (11:8–9).
settings.readers: For Israel, Babel was Babylon, whose great temple tower was called the house of the foundation of heaven and earth. Exiles who saw that tower heard the story mock the empire's pride: God has to come down even to see it. The next chapter gives the answer. God himself will make Abram's name great (12:2).
views: Most readers see the scattering as a punishment.
Others note that the builders refused to spread out and fill the earth (1:28; 11:4), so the scattering does what God intended.
